name: Amoeba Music
blurb: Californian record shops founded on Telegraph Avenue, Berkeley, in 1990; San Francisco opened in 1997 and Hollywood in 2001.

name: Buy-Rite Records
blurb: Cliff Thomas's west-side Detroit shop, the city's main source of Chicago house and ghetto-house twelve-inches.

name: Dance Tracks
blurb: East 3rd Street deep-house shop run by Stan Hatzakis, then Joe Claussell and Stefan Prescott; closed 30 November 2007.

name: The Diskery
blurb: Birmingham shop opened by Morris Hunting in 1952; at 99 Bromsgrove Street from 1972, on Bristol Street by 2024. Its imported R&B 45s drew mods.

name: FON Records
blurb: Sheffield's shop and studio before Warp, where the bleep records were sold and some were made.

name: Honest Jon's
blurb: Portobello Road shop begun in a Golborne Road butcher's; James Lavelle and Gilles Peterson worked its counter, and it has run a label since 2002.

name: Kristina Records
blurb: Opened at 44 Stoke Newington Road by Jason Spinks, Jack Rollo and Jamie Thornington; left Dalston in August 2018, reopening on Well Street in 2019.

name: Manchester Underground
blurb: Corn Exchange basement shop opened by three former Spin Inn staff; the 1996 bomb closed its first premises.

name: Piccadilly Records
blurb: Manchester shop that began as a department-store record counter in Piccadilly Plaza and has traded at 53 Oldham Street since 1997.

name: Rhythm Division
blurb: Roman Road shop in Bow tied to the growth of grime, where MCs played dubplates and Wiley filmed a video; a coffee shop replaced it.

name: Rubadub
blurb: Glasgow shop and distributor, begun in Paisley, that imports Detroit, Chicago and New York labels and sells synthesisers at 35 Howard Street.

name: Space Hall
blurb: Kreuzberg shop spread over Zossener Straße 33–35, with house and techno in a dim back room joined to the rest in 2009.

name: Technique
blurb: Shibuya dance-vinyl shop at Udagawacho 33-14, popular with travelling DJs; it moved into Parco in 2020 and shut its doors in March 2022.

name: Vinyl Exchange
blurb: Second-hand shop at 18 Oldham Street, Manchester, whose staff have included Dave Booth and Balearic Mike.

name: Aba Shanti-I
blurb: Dub and roots system that has played Notting Hill Carnival for nearly thirty years, at East Row and Southern Row.

name: Britannia Row Productions
blurb: PA hire company formed by Pink Floyd in 1975 and bought out in 1984; flew 50kW of Turbosound Flashlight at Glastonbury in 1994.

name: d&b audiotechnik
blurb: German loudspeaker maker founded by Jürgen Daubert and Rolf Belz; its Cardioid Subwoofer Array arrived in 2004, the J-Series in 2006.

name: Duke Reid the Trojan
blurb: Former police sergeant Duke Reid's sound, crowned King of Sounds and Blues in the mid-1950s; rival of Coxsone Dodd's Downbeat.

name: Tubby's Hometown Hi-Fi
blurb: King Tubby's own sound, built on his amplifiers, known for echo and reverb and for launching U-Roy; police wrecked it in 1975.

name: Martin Audio
blurb: Dave Martin's London loudspeaker firm of 1971: Pink Floyd's bass bins, the Philishave mid horn and, by 2010–11, award-winning club sound at Ministry of Sound.

name: Richard Long & Associates
blurb: The Paradise Garage system designer: the Levan horns, the bass array, the sound the whole genre was built to be played on.

name: Smokescreen Soundsystem
blurb: Sheffield free-party house system, formed about two years after DiY, that moved to Nottingham in 1997 and kept its parties small after 1994.

name: Turbosound
